column1: # Step 4's prohibitions: the dodges that would make m2 and m3 look satisfied.
# The split is rung3.tsv's. A *requirement* says the work was done; a
# *prohibition* says it was not faked, and a prohibition is priced at the whole
# reward because a faked step is worth nothing at all. So "ANSI is on" lives in
# m04.tsv and is worth its share, and the nine rules here are the ways a
# candidate could get that share without doing the step. Two were added by the
# static review's round 1, three by its round 2 and one by its round 3
#   the reflection dodge   m2 reads the jar for `org/apache/spark/SparkConf` in
#                          the constant pool, and a SparkConf built by
#                          reflection is not there -- it is a *string*. The
#                          class name does not appear as a string constant
#                          anywhere in the start tree's jar (measured), so this
#                          rule costs an honest candidate nothing. Same shape
#                          and same reason as cheats3.tsv's no-describe-reflect.
#   the system-property    A SparkConf loads every `spark.*` JVM system property
#   dodge                  that is set when it is constructed, so one
#                          `System.setProperty("spark.sql.ansi.enabled",
#                          "true")` in a static initializer puts the dialect on
#                          every session in the JVM -- including the ones this
#                          step is asking the candidate to create and has not.
#                          It is the one route to m3 that does not pass through
#                          the entry point m2 is about. This codebase sets no
#                          system property at all, in src/main or src/test --
#                          0 occurrences of setProperty, setProperties or
#                          getProperties on any receiver, measured on the handed
#                          tree and the golden one -- so the rule is scoped to
#                          the whole call and costs an honest candidate nothing.
#                          Two rules, because the receiver on an `ast.call` row
#                          is syntax. `System.setProperty(...)` names System;
#                          `System.getProperties().setProperty(...)` does the
#                          same thing and names `System.getProperties()`, and
#                          assigning that table to a local first names the
#                          local. What every route has in common is that it
#                          reaches the table through `System`, so the second
#                          rule prohibits reaching it at all. Round 2 of the
#                          static review found the first hole.
#   the gate's own class   GateProbe is on the driver class path, in the
#                          candidate's JVM, and its dump is guarded by a
#                          counter that fires once. Candidate code that calls
#                          `gate.GateProbe.dump()` early spends that counter,
#                          so the listener's own dump is a no-op and whatever
#                          the candidate writes on the descriptor afterwards is
#                          the whole file -- with no real rows to land beside
#                          the invented ones, which is the signature the
#                          forged-row rule below depends on. cheats.tsv
#                          prohibits *shipping* a `gate/*` class and prohibits
#                          the class name appearing as a string constant;
#                          neither reads a direct call, which is a methodref
#                          and not a string. This does. The same hole is open
#                          at steps 2 and 3, whose review rounds are spent
#   the dropped program    Every rule over the per-program kinds is `absent`, so
#                          a program that reported nothing satisfies all of
#                          them, and on the handed tree 29 of the 96 report a
#                          red row. Deleting those 29 files is therefore worth
#                          more than migrating the 29 programs. A probe file
#                          exists for every job that started a SparkContext, so
#                          test.sh can tell a program that never reached one --
#                          17 of this census's 140 jobs, every one an
#                          argument-validation exit, and exactly one of those
#                          exiting 0 -- from a file that was removed, and seeds
#                          the second as `appsession <label> dropped`. This is
#                          the rule that prices it.
#   the store-assignment   ANSI mode changes two things: how expressions
#   dodge                  evaluate, and how values cast on insert. The second
#                          is governed by spark.sql.storeAssignmentPolicy, which
#                          is already ANSI by default here -- measured as ANSI on
#                          all 124 probe files of the step-3 oracle run. Setting
#                          it to LEGACY buys back exactly the casting behaviour
#                          the step is adopting, while leaving `ansi.enabled`
#                          reading true for m3 to find. Both reads are guarded:
#                          the setconf one because that is where a candidate
#                          would write it, the conf one because that is where it
#                          would take effect.
#   the forged probe row   GateProbe runs inside the candidate's driver JVM and
#                          writes on a descriptor that is open in it, so rows
#                          can be appended to a probe file and a probe file can
#                          be rewritten. Nothing on this side of the wall can
#                          stop that. What it cannot do is stop the real rows
#                          from landing beside the invented ones: GateProbe
#                          emits each of its own `probe` keys exactly once per
#                          JVM, so a second `app.label` or a second
#                          `session.present` in one file is a row something
#                          other than GateProbe put there. probe-derive.py
#                          reports that as `appsession <label> tampered`. Round
#                          2 of the static review found the same reasoning
#                          missing on the `setconf` rows, which come from
#                          `conf.getAll()` filtered to spark.sql.* and are
#                          therefore a map -- once per key per dump, so a
#                          repeat is a forgery there too. The `conf` rows are
#                          the one kind where a repeat is legitimate, and they
#                          are handled the other way: a repeat that disagrees
#                          becomes `<disagreement>`, which no rule reads as
#                          good. Measured across the 246 recorded probe files
#                          of the before and gold suites: 0 repeats of either
#                          kind and 0 disagreements (NOTES 6.4.9). It reports
#                          tampering before it applies the filter that
#                          skips the harness's own jobs -- otherwise writing
#                          `app.label HarnessDriver-x` as the first row of your
#                          own file would be the way past it.
#                          This is a backstop, not the defence. The defence is
#                          that every rule over the derived kinds is `absent`,
#                          so a forged row can only add a reading to a rule
#                          that fails on readings (m04.tsv).
#   the unattributable row Round 3 of the static review took the same question
#                          one step past the file: the runner and every job of
#                          the replay share one uid, so a later job could empty
#                          or rewrite an earlier job's probe file, and an
#                          `absent` rule reads an emptied file as a clean one.
#                          So the files are no longer written on that side of
#                          the wall at all. Root drains one fifo for the whole
#                          replay and names each job's rows by a token it
#                          issued to that job and recorded on a descriptor the
#                          job does not inherit (gates/probe-split.py). A
#                          process that outlives its job still holds the pipe,
#                          but it holds its own token: its rows land in its own
#                          file, beside the real ones, where a repeated key is
#                          the forgery above. Rows carrying a token nobody was
#                          issued belong to no job and are not given to one --
#                          attributing a forgery to a program would be the same
#                          mistake in the other direction. They are collected
#                          under the label `stray`, which no job in jobs.tsv
#                          has and no plan can produce, and this is the rule
#                          that prices them. A stray file is a reading nobody
#                          can stand behind, so m2-session-live goes red on it
#                          too; two rules saying the channel is void is not a
#                          double charge, it is the same void seen from the
#                          two sides that look at it.
# The conf-side rule carries the `<unset>` exclusion the other conf rules carry
# (cheats3.tsv): an angle-bracketed value is the probe failing to read, not a
# candidate setting something, and GateProbe already reports that separately as
# an `error` fact for common.tsv's probe-clean to catch.
no-sparkconf-reflect
column5: the jar carries SparkConf's class name as a string constant, which is how a class gets constructed by reflection when the constant pool is being read for its absence

column1: no-storeassignment-loosened-set
column5: a replayed job set the store-assignment policy away from ANSI, which buys back the casting behaviour ANSI mode was adopted to replace

column1: no-storeassignment-loosened-conf
column5: a live session ran with the store-assignment policy away from ANSI, so ANSI mode was on in name while the casting rules it governs were not in force

column1: no-system-property-spark
column5: a JVM system property is set from the sources; a SparkConf reads every spark.* system property when it is built, so this installs a Spark setting on sessions the step asked the candidate to write rather than on the ones they did

column1: no-system-property-table
column5: the JVM's system-property table is reached from the sources, which is the same dodge as setting one directly with the receiver spelled differently; this codebase never asks for it

column1: no-gate-class-ref
column5: the jar under test calls into this verifier's own observer; a candidate class that can reach GateProbe can spend its once-per-JVM dump before the listener does and leave the file to be written by something else

column1: no-dropped-program
column5: a program that finished successfully left no probe file behind, so nothing this gate asks about it can be answered; every per-program rule is absent and silence would satisfy all of them

column1: no-probe-row-forgery
column5: a probe file carries two of a key the listener writes once per JVM, so rows in it were written by something other than the listener and no reading taken from that file means anything

column1: no-probe-stray
column5: rows arrived on the replay's probe channel carrying a token no job was issued, so something wrote on it that the runner never handed a place in the reading, and no file it did hand out can be trusted to be only its own
